cards.title: Bond enthalpy sums: broken minus formed, every bond counted

walkthrough.question: Hydrogen is made industrially from natural gas and steam: CH4(g) + H2O(g) → 3H2(g) + CO(g). Use average bond enthalpies from the data booklet, with C≡O taken as 1077 kJ mol−1, to find ΔH for this reaction in kJ.
walkthrough.key_idea: ΔH equals bonds broken minus bonds formed, counting every bond.
walkthrough.careful: Count bonds per molecule, then multiply by the coefficient.
procedure: Draw each molecule and list its bonds.
Multiply each bond count by the molecule's coefficient.
Read each bond enthalpy from the booklet.
Add up bonds broken, then bonds formed.
Subtract: broken minus formed.
Give the sign and the unit.
tricks: Water has two O–H bonds and CO2 two C=O: multiply first.
Check the sign: larger broken total means positive ΔH.
if_lost: Which bonds are in one CH4 molecule?
How many O–H bonds does one water molecule have?
Which side of the equation has its bonds broken?
Which total comes first in the subtraction?

1_context.short: Standard marks-rich calculation, built from a booklet lookup.
1_context.why: Bonds are the only energy terms used, so each bond counted carries straight through to the answer.
1_context.avoid: Reaching for formation data here; part (b) asks for that separately.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: calculate the enthalpy change of a reaction from average bond enthalpy data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use small molecules with bonds drawn. Exams expect you to count bonds yourself from formulas.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Broken 2582, formed 2385, then the signed difference: three marks.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each sum is its own mark, so visible working still scores if a later step slips.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Formed minus broken: 06N.2.SL.TZ0.2 and 12N.2.SL.TZ0.2 both report this reversal.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The last mark needs the right subtraction: a negative result cannot be correct here.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Both sums right with the subtraction reversed misses the final mark. Right direction and sign earns all three.

3_novel_application.short: Industry story hides a plain broken-minus-formed sum.
3_novel_application.why: Context changes nothing. Only the species and their bonds matter, and the given value replaces a lookup.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using C–O or C=O because CO looks like a carbonyl; it is given as triple.
3_novel_application.disguise: An industrial hydrogen process with an unusual triple-bonded product, CO.
3_novel_application.heuristic: If a bond table is called for, ignore the story and tally bonds.

4_command_terms.short: Determine: one value, but each sum earns its own mark.
4_command_terms.why: The final mark rewards only sign and subtraction; the sums score on their own.
4_command_terms.avoid: Writing just a final number: one slip then loses everything.
4_command_terms.demands: Reach the single value from bond data, showing both totals.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Three marks: one each for broken total, formed total and signed final value.

5_time_efficiency.short: Tally, sum twice, subtract: under two minutes.
5_time_efficiency.why: A written tally prevents the forgotten-bond error examiners report most often.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Drawing full three-dimensional shapes; 06M.2.SL.TZ0.1 needs only the bond counts.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip shapes, lone pairs and any comment on the reaction type.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 12 gives all values; the subtraction rule you memorise.
6_data_booklet.why: The booklet supplies numbers only, so the direction of subtraction is the whole memory load.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Taking C–O (358) or C=O (804) instead of the triple bond value.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 12: C–H 414, O–H 463, H–H 436, C≡O 1077 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Broken minus formed is NOT in the supplied section text.

7_elimination.short: A negative answer is out: broken clearly outweighs formed.
7_elimination.why: A rough tally, about 2600 against 2400, fixes the sign before any exact arithmetic.
7_elimination.avoid: Assuming every reaction is exothermic; this one absorbs energy.

definitely_wrong.rule: The rough broken total exceeds the rough formed total.

definitely_wrong.target: a value using product bonds only
definitely_wrong.rule: Reactant bonds must break, so both sides must appear.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: calculate ΔH from average bond enthalpy data.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show the formula on simple molecules. Exams make you count bonds in larger species, where forgotten bonds cost the most.

trap_boundaries: Formed minus broken reverses the sign (06N.2.SL.TZ0.2, 12N.2.SL.TZ0.2).
Forgotten bonds such as C–C spoil a sum (16N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
Water's two O–H bonds and CO2's two C=O are often undercounted (06M.2.SL.TZ0.1, 15N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial credit comes from correct sums. Full credit needs both totals, the right direction and the sign.

disguises: Industrial process context
An unusual bond value supplied in the stem
MCQ options left as unevaluated expressions (19M.1.HL.TZ2.14)
3_novel_application.heuristic: A bond table means broken minus formed, whatever the story.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark per sum and one for the signed final value; ECF is reported in 10M.2.SL.TZ2.4 and 08N.2.SL.TZ0.4.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip shapes and lone pairs; a tally is enough.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 12 gives single and multiple bonds separately. Check the bond order before reading. Broken minus formed is NOT in the supplied section text.

rules: Estimate both totals first to fix the sign.
In an MCQ, an option with the same numbers but opposite sign is the reversal trap (14N.1.HL.TZ0.15, 19M.1.HL.TZ2.14).

cards.title: Why bond enthalpy answers are less accurate: averages, not these compounds

walkthrough.question: For CH4(g) + H2O(g) → 3H2(g) + CO(g), ΔH was found twice: once from bond enthalpies and once from a table of ΔHf values. Outline why the value from bond enthalpies is the less accurate one.
walkthrough.key_idea: Bond enthalpies are averages, not values specific to these compounds.
walkthrough.question_type: Why bond enthalpy values differ from others
walkthrough.careful: Say averaged over similar compounds; experimental error is not the reason.
procedure: Name the two data sources being compared.
State bond values are averaged over similar compounds.
State they are therefore not specific to these compounds.
Check for liquids: a state change adds another difference.
tricks: Mention states only if a liquid appears; here all species are gases.
if_lost: What does the word average tell you about a table value?
Was each bond value measured in this actual molecule?
Which data set belongs to the exact compounds in the equation?

1_context.short: A reasoning mark: why the bond table is a weaker source.
1_context.why: Formation values belong to the actual compounds, so the averaged bond table is the weak link.
1_context.avoid: Discussing the reaction itself; both numbers describe the same reaction.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: explain why bond enthalpy data are average values and may differ from experiment.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books give 'average' as a definition. Exams make you use it as the reason for a difference.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Either 'averaged values' or 'not specific to these compounds' earns it.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Both say the same thing: the table value was not measured in these particular molecules.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Repeating the question: 09M.2.SL.TZ1.2 reports answers giving no reason for the accuracy difference.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: State changes earn credit only where liquids appear (18M.2.HL.TZ1.3); here all species are gases.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark, no partial credit: name averaging, not merely 'less accurate'.

3_novel_application.short: Looks like arithmetic; it really asks about the data source.
3_novel_application.why: The two numbers do not matter. Only where each data set comes from matters.
3_novel_application.avoid: Explaining from the size of the gap between the two answers.
3_novel_application.disguise: It follows two calculations, so it looks like a numerical comparison.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which data set was measured on these exact compounds.

4_command_terms.short: Outline: one brief reason, no calculation.
4_command_terms.why: A brief account fits one mark; a longer one cannot earn more.
4_command_terms.avoid: Repeating a calculation: 09M.2.SL.TZ1.2 saw this where reasoning was wanted.
4_command_terms.demands: Give a short reason about the bond values.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one valid reason.

5_time_efficiency.short: One clause, fifteen seconds, move on.
5_time_efficiency.why: A one-mark outline should not take longer than writing one line.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Re-checking the earlier calculations at this point.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the numbers and any talk of measurement error.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 12's heading says average; the reason you memorise.
6_data_booklet.why: The heading gives you the word. The reason behind it must come from you.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Blaming the booklet's precision; averaging is the reason.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 12 is headed bond enthalpies or average bond enthalpies; section 13 lists values per compound.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Averaged over similar compounds: NOT in the supplied section text.

7_elimination.short: No experiment here, so heat loss cannot be the reason.
7_elimination.why: Both values come from data tables. 10N.2.HL.TZ0.4 reports heat loss being wrongly used as a reason.
7_elimination.avoid: Answering about hydrogen's element status; that is a different part.

definitely_wrong.rule: No experiment is described in this question.

definitely_wrong.target: restating that it is less accurate
definitely_wrong.rule: That repeats the stem and gives no reason.

walkthrough.answer: Bond enthalpies are averages over similar compounds, so they are not specific to the compounds in this reaction.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: why bond enthalpy data are average values and may differ from experiment.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books define the term. Exams ask you to apply it as a cause, often after a comparison calculation.

trigger_phrases: formation values are specific to the compound
trap_boundaries: Liquid products need condensation or vaporization considered (18M.2.HL.TZ1.3, 09M.2.SL.TZ1.2, 16N.2.SL.TZ0.1).
'Similar' is often omitted in definitions (11N.2.HL.TZ0.3, 08N.2.HL.TZ0.5).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Saying only 'less accurate' scores nothing. Naming averaged, non-specific values scores.

disguises: Comes straight after two calculations
Reworded as 'why do the two answers differ?'
3_novel_application.heuristic: Compare the data sources, not the numbers.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark for one valid reason; no working needed.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not re-derive or quote the two numbers.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 12 is headed bond enthalpies or average bond enthalpies; section 13 lists values compound by compound.

rules: With no experiment described, heat loss cannot be the cause.
Check states before citing them: if all species are gases, state changes do not apply.

evidence.note: Part (b)(iii) asks why the bond enthalpy value is less accurate.
Accepts averaged values or values not specific to these compounds.
Specific ΔHf against averaged bond values; condensation added where a liquid forms.
Many repeated the question, giving no reason for the accuracy difference.
Candidates struggled to explain what average means.
Averaging over similar compounds was very rarely mentioned.

cards.title: Bond enthalpy equations: gas to gaseous atoms, one mole of bonds

walkthrough.question:
Pick the equation that shows the average bond enthalpy of the Si–H bond in silane.
A. SiH4(g) → SiH3(g) + H(g)
B. ¼SiH4(g) → ¼Si(g) + H(g)
C. SiH4(g) → SiH3(g) + ½H2(g)
D. SiH4(g) → Si(g) + 4H(g)
walkthrough.key_idea: Average bond enthalpy breaks one mole of bonds, gas to gaseous atoms.
walkthrough.question_type: Which equation represents a bond enthalpy
walkthrough.careful: Average over all bonds means one mole of bonds broken.
procedure: Check every species is gaseous.
Check the products are atoms, not molecules or ions.
Count how many moles of the bond break.
For an average, divide the whole molecule by bonds present.
tricks: Any H2 product means a bond forms, so reject it.
A whole-molecule equation has about four times the bond value in SiH4.
if_lost: What state must all species be in?
Should the products be atoms or molecules?
How many Si–H bonds break in each option?
How many moles of bonds should the equation break?

1_context.short: Definition test written as an equation choice.
1_context.why: The definition has three checks: gas, atoms, one mole of bonds. Each option fails one or more.
1_context.avoid: Thinking breaking one bond in one molecule is the average.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: bond-breaking absorbs energy; average values are used.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books test the wording. Exams test it as an equation, with fractions for the average.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only one option has gas atoms and one mole of bonds.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Average means the total for all four bonds shared out, so one quarter of the molecule.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: D: 09M.1.SL.TZ1.16 reports a whole-molecule option attracting many, despite about four times the value.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The mark stops at the amount: gaseous atoms are not enough if four moles of bonds break.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The correct option breaks one mole of bonds; D breaks four, giving four times the value.

3_novel_application.short: Unfamiliar silane and a fraction hide a standard definition.
3_novel_application.why: Silicon behaves like carbon here: four equal bonds. The fraction just scales the molecule down.
3_novel_application.avoid: Rejecting B because a quarter of a molecule looks odd.
3_novel_application.disguise: A silicon compound and a fractional coefficient.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask how many moles of the named bond break in each equation.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: an all-or-nothing choice.
4_command_terms.why: One mark depends on the correct equation, so every check must pass.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping at the first gaseous option; all four are gaseous.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the one equation that fits the definition.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check products, then amount: thirty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: All species are gaseous here, so the state check removes nothing. Go to products and amount.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Calculating any value; no numbers are needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the booklet's Si–H value: it does not affect the choice.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 12 lists Si–H; the definition you memorise.
6_data_booklet.why: The table gives a number, never the process it describes.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting the booklet for an equation; the supplied section gives only values.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 12 lists Si–H at 323 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Gas molecule to gaseous atoms, one mole of bonds: NOT in the supplied section text.

7_elimination.short: A, C and D each fail one definition check.
7_elimination.why: A breaks only the first bond, C forms H2 and D breaks four moles of bonds.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping A: the first bond need not equal the average.

definitely_wrong.rule: Breaks only the first bond, so it is not an average.
H2 forms a new bond, so products are not all atoms.
Breaks four moles of bonds, so four times too large.

walkthrough.answer: B. One quarter of the molecule breaks one mole of Si–H bonds, giving gaseous atoms.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.1: bond-breaking absorbs energy; bond enthalpies are average values.
1_context.textbook_gap: Definition questions look easy, but this idea has produced some of the lowest correct rates in the pack.

trap_boundaries: 'Gaseous' is very often omitted (08N.2.SL.TZ0.4, 12N.2.SL.TZ0.2, 11N.2.HL.TZ0.3).
Average means from a range of similar compounds (09M.2.SL.TZ2.6).
Liquids stop a bond-enthalpy-only calculation (15M.1.HL.TZ2.15).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A gaseous-atoms equation with the wrong amount misses the mark; only one mole of bonds qualifies.

disguises: Unfamiliar molecule with fractional coefficients
Asked as 'which ΔH can be found from bond data alone?' (15M.1.HL.TZ2.15)
3_novel_application.heuristic: Scan state symbols first: bond enthalpies apply only to gases.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing. Written definitions often carry two marks, for gaseous and for average (12N.2.SL.TZ0.2).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: No values are needed for a definition choice.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 12 gives values only. The definition is NOT in the supplied section text and must be memorised.

rules: Any liquid or solid: not a bond enthalpy process alone.
Any molecule in the products other than a fragment: a bond forms, so reject it. Exception: stepwise A-type equations show one bond, not an average.

evidence.note: Average Si–H equation, answer B.
35% correct; a whole-molecule option attracted many despite four times the value.
10.82% correct on a bond enthalpy definition question.
Liquid ethanol needs more than bond data; 65% correct.
Same idea at SL, 52% correct.

cards.title: Hess's law from equations: flip, scale, then add

walkthrough.question:
Two reactions are given: Fe2O3(s) + CO(g) → 2FeO(s) + CO2(g), ΔH = −3 kJ, and Fe(s) + CO2(g) → FeO(s) + CO(g), ΔH = +11 kJ. Find ΔH, in kJ, for Fe2O3(s) + 3CO(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3CO2(g).
A. −25
B. −14
C. +8
D. +19
walkthrough.key_idea: Flip and scale the given equations to match the target, then add.
walkthrough.careful: Scale ΔH whenever you scale the equation.
procedure: Find each target species in one given equation.
Reverse an equation if a species is on the wrong side.
Change ΔH's sign when you reverse.
Multiply to match the target coefficient; multiply ΔH too.
Add the equations; check they cancel to the target.
Add the adjusted ΔH values.
tricks: A species absent from the target must cancel: use it to set the multiplier.
Check options for the unscaled sum: that is the usual distractor.
if_lost: Which side of the target is Fe on?
Which side is Fe on in the given equation?
Which species is in both givens but not the target?
How many moles of that species must cancel?

1_context.short: Core Hess skill, set almost every year as an MCQ.
1_context.why: Enthalpy depends only on start and end states, so equations can be added like algebra.
1_context.avoid: Thinking this is a Born-Haber problem: 16M.1.SL.TZ0.14 notes the difference.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.2: apply Hess's law to calculate enthalpy changes in multistep reactions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show two-step cycles with neat numbers. Exams need one equation reversed and doubled at once.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Reverse and double the second equation, then add it to the first.
2_markscheme_logic.why: 2FeO made in the first equation must be used up, which fixes the factor of two.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: B: 18N.1.HL.TZ0.14 reports this distractor, from not multiplying the second reaction by two.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A flip alone is not enough: the mark needs the factor of two as well.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct: −3 + 2(−11). Tempting B: −3 + (−11), which leaves FeO uncancelled.

3_novel_application.short: Unfamiliar iron oxides, but FeO just needs to cancel.
3_novel_application.why: FeO is not in the target, so the equations must make and remove equal amounts.
3_novel_application.avoid: Trying to use FeO's formation data; none is needed.
3_novel_application.disguise: An iron oxide intermediate that never appears in the target.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Find the species missing from the target and make it cancel.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: one letter, no method marks.
4_command_terms.why: Working earns nothing in Paper 1A, so a quick sign and factor check protects the mark.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trusting a matching option: the wrong factor also lands on one.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the one correct enthalpy value.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Fix the flip and the factor: under a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: Only the second equation needs changing, so there is one manipulation to write.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Rewriting all equations in full when one line of arithmetic will do.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip naming the reactions; no chemistry beyond the equations matters.

6_data_booklet.short: Nothing to look up: every ΔH is in the stem.
6_data_booklet.why: The method is pure manipulation, so there are no booklet values to read.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up iron oxide values; they are not needed.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None needed; the stem supplies every enthalpy.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Reversing changes the sign; multiplying scales ΔH. NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Positive answers go: both contributions must be negative.
7_elimination.why: −3 stays and +11 flips negative, so nothing positive can result.
7_elimination.avoid: Forgetting to flip +11, which is what makes positive answers tempting.

definitely_wrong.rule: Both adjusted terms are negative, so the sum cannot be positive.
Both adjusted terms are negative, so the sum cannot be positive.
It adds −3 and −11 with no factor, leaving FeO uncancelled.

1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.2: apply Hess's law in multistep reactions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use simple addition. Exams combine a reversal, a multiplier and sometimes algebraic letters.

trap_boundaries: Forgetting a factor of two is the leading distractor (18N.1.HL.TZ0.14).
Forgetting to halve also costs: nearly 20% in 15M.1.HL.TZ2.14.
Algebraic letters are normal in Paper 1 because no calculator is allowed (11N.1.HL.TZ0.16, 12M.1.SL.TZ1.16).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Right chemistry with a missed multiplier lands on a listed wrong answer; only sign and factor together score.

disguises: Unfamiliar oxides as intermediates
Letters instead of numbers
Target given as a word description
3_novel_application.heuristic: Use the species missing from the target to set the multiplier.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing; written answers give ECF on a correct cycle (25N.2.HL.6221.5).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not write every balanced line twice; note flip and factor beside each given.

6_data_booklet.hack: Enthalpies come from the stem. The reversal and scaling rules are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Add adjusted signs first: same-sign terms cannot give the opposite sign.
An option equal to the unscaled sum is the forgot-the-factor trap.

evidence.note: Three-quarters correct; distractor B omitted the factor of two.
68% correct; nearly 20% forgot to divide by two.
Letter version, about 90% correct.
Sulfur oxides with a doubled equation.
Noted as Hess's law rather than Born-Haber; 60% correct.
Explains why Paper 1 uses letter variables.

cards.title: Hess cycles from a diagram: same start, same end

walkthrough.question:
A cycle has CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g) across the top, with enthalpy change ΔH. Each side then reacts with 2HCl(aq) and an arrow runs down to the shared product CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g): ΔH1 from CaCO3(s) and ΔH2 from CaO(s) + CO2(g). Which expression gives ΔH?
A. ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2
B. ΔH = 2ΔH1 − ΔH2
C. ΔH = ΔH1 − 2ΔH2
D. ΔH = ΔH1 + ΔH2
walkthrough.key_idea: Two routes with the same start and end have equal enthalpy.
walkthrough.question_type: Hess's law: read a cycle diagram
walkthrough.careful: An arrow travelled backwards is subtracted, not added.
procedure: Mark the start and end of the unknown arrow.
Find a second route using the other arrows.
Add arrows travelled in their own direction.
Subtract arrows travelled backwards.
Set that route equal to the unknown.
tricks: Trace with your finger: each arrow is used once, coefficients in reagents are not multipliers.
if_lost: Where does the unknown arrow start and end?
Which arrow leaves that start along the other route?
Does the second arrow point with your route or against it?

1_context.short: Reading a cycle, no equations to combine.
1_context.why: Both reactions can be measured with acid, so the unmeasurable decomposition follows from their difference.
1_context.avoid: Writing formation equations; the diagram holds everything needed.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.2: enthalpy change is independent of the pathway between initial and final states.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show cycles as a statement of the law. Exams present them in unfamiliar layouts and ask for an expression.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Go down with ΔH1, then back up against ΔH2.
2_markscheme_logic.why: From CaCO3 the other route reaches the shared product, then returns to CaO + CO2 against ΔH2.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: D: adding both forgets that ΔH2's arrow is travelled backwards.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: No factor of two appears: 2HCl is in both arrows and each arrow is used once.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct: one arrow forward, one reversed. D adds both; B and C wrongly double one.

3_novel_application.short: Lab reactions with acid hide a plain two-route cycle.
3_novel_application.why: The acid is only a bridge to a common product. Its identity does not affect the expression.
3_novel_application.avoid: Being distracted by CO2 appearing on both sides; it changes nothing.
3_novel_application.disguise: An acid-based route to a thermal decomposition, in an unusual layout.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Name start and end, then ignore every chemical label.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose the expression only.
4_command_terms.why: An expression needs no numbers, so the mark depends on direction alone.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trying to find numerical values; none are given.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the expression that matches the cycle.

cards.title: Born-Haber terms as equations: states and amounts decide

walkthrough.question:
Pick the equation for bromine's atomization enthalpy under standard conditions.
A. ½Br2(l) → Br(g)
B. Br2(l) → 2Br(g)
C. Br2(l) → 2Br(l)
D. ½Br2(l) → Br(l)
walkthrough.key_idea: Atomization: standard-state element to one mole of gaseous atoms.
walkthrough.question_type: Which equation represents a Born-Haber term
walkthrough.careful: Check the state at both ends, then the amount.
procedure: Name the term's required start and end.
Check the starting species and its state.
Check the final species and its state.
Check the amount: one mole of what?
tricks: Halving bond enthalpy works for gases like Cl2. Fails for Br2(l), a liquid.
Lattice equations always go solid to gaseous ions.
if_lost: What state does bromine have under standard conditions?
What state must atomized products be in?
How many moles of atoms does atomization define?

1_context.short: Recall tested through states, and it trips many candidates.
1_context.why: The term fixes the amount of atoms formed, which is a different rule from bond breaking.
1_context.avoid: Thinking one mole of Br2 is the base unit.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.5: the cycle includes enthalpy of atomization, from sublimation and/or bond enthalpies.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books mention atomization as a label. Exams test it as one balanced equation with exact states.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Half a mole of liquid Br2 gives one mole of gaseous atoms.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The definition counts per mole of atoms formed, so half a mole of Br2 is enough.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: B: gives two moles of atoms. Also 09M.2.HL.TZ1.6 reports this process mislabelled as vaporization.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Two moles of atoms is double the term, even with correct states.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A forms one mole of gaseous atoms; B forms two, so its value is doubled.

3_novel_application.short: Bromine's liquid state is the twist here.
3_novel_application.why: Bromine starts as a liquid, so atomization includes vaporization, and bond enthalpy alone falls short.
3_novel_application.avoid: Writing Br2(g) as the start, which ignores bromine's standard state.
3_novel_application.disguise: A halogen that is not a gas under standard conditions.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask the element's standard state, then ask for one mole of gas atoms.

4_command_terms.why: One mark, and three checks per option, so scanning is quicker than recalling words.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping at the first option with gaseous atoms.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the equation fitting the definition.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.why: The product check removes half of the options immediately.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Using booklet values, which are not needed.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip section 12: no values are asked for.

6_data_booklet.pattern: None for atomization; section 16 words the lattice process only.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Atomization forms one mole of gaseous atoms: NOT in the supplied section text.

7_elimination.avoid: Keeping B because its states are right.

Atoms must be gaseous, not liquid.

cards.title: Experimental ΔH: sign from temperature, moles from the equation

walkthrough.question:
Solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, 0.050 mol, is added to 50 cm3 of 2.0 mol dm−3 citric acid solution: C6H8O7(aq) + 3NaHCO3(s) → C6H5O7Na3(aq) + 3CO2(g) + 3H2O(l). The temperature falls from 298 K to 297 K. With c = 4.18 J g−1 K−1 and Q = mcΔT, what is the enthalpy of this reaction in kJ mol−1?
A. +4.18
B. −4.18
C. +12.5
D. −12.5
walkthrough.key_idea: Falling temperature means positive; scale per mole of equation as written.
walkthrough.question_type: Calorimetry data: find enthalpy per mole
walkthrough.careful: Use the mass of solution; scale to the equation's coefficient.
procedure: Find Q using the mass of the solution.
Find moles of the limiting reactant.
Divide Q by moles; convert J to kJ.
Scale to the coefficient in the equation.
Temperature fell: positive; temperature rose: negative.
tricks: Set the sign from the temperature first: it removes half the options.
A coefficient of three is the factor between the two sizes offered.
if_lost: Did the solution warm up or cool down?
What mass goes into Q = mcΔT?
Which reactant runs out first?
How many moles of NaHCO3 does the equation show?

1_context.short: Lab data turned into ΔH per mole of equation.
1_context.why: Heat is measured for the amount used, so it must be scaled to the amounts in the equation.
1_context.avoid: Stopping at per mole of NaHCO3; the equation has three.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.1.4: calculate ΔH from Q = mcΔT. Filed under R1.2 as data work.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use a one-to-one neutralization. This question has a three-to-one equation and a falling temperature.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Positive sign and scaling by three give the right option.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The sign comes from cooling and the size from 4.18 kJ per mole, tripled for the equation.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: D: the sign is overlooked. 25M.1A.SL.TZ2.16 reports the same kind of sign slip after correct numbers.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Right size with the wrong sign is D; right sign without scaling is A.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C has positive sign and factor of three; A misses three and D misses the sign.

3_novel_application.short: Unfamiliar acid; the numbers work like any calorimetry problem.
3_novel_application.why: The formula of citric acid matters only through its coefficient, which sets the limiting reactant.
3_novel_application.avoid: Including the solid's mass or citric acid's molar mass.
3_novel_application.disguise: A complex organic acid and a three-to-one equation.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which reactant limits, then read its coefficient.

4_command_terms.short: No command term: choose one signed value.
4_command_terms.why: Sign and size each split the options, so both checks are required.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.short: Sign first, then size: about a minute.
5_time_efficiency.why: The sign removes two options, and only then does the factor of three matter.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing full working; the numbers are simple without a calculator.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip converting 298 K; only the one-degree difference matters.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet needed: c and Q = mcΔT are in the stem.
6_data_booklet.why: The stem supplies the constant and formula, so memory only covers method.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None needed; the stem supplies c and the formula.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Sign from temperature change and scaling to the equation: NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Negative options go: the temperature fell.
7_elimination.why: A falling temperature means the reaction absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive with no arithmetic.
7_elimination.avoid: Reading a loss of temperature as a loss of energy from the reaction.

definitely_wrong.rule: Temperature fell, so ΔH cannot be negative.
Temperature fell, so ΔH cannot be negative.

walkthrough.answer: C. Q = 50 × 4.18 × 1 = 209 J for 0.050 mol, so 4.18 kJ per mole of NaHCO3; three moles in the equation gives +12.5 kJ mol−1.

1_context.syllabus_hook: Filed under R1.2 in the pack as data work; the Q = mcΔT method belongs to R1.1.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use one-to-one reactions. Exams use unusual coefficients and endothermic changes.

trap_boundaries: Using solid mass rather than water's, or adding 273 to ΔT (11M.2.SL.TZ2.1).
Forgetting J to kJ and the sign (11M.2.SL.TZ2.1, 11M.2.HL.TZ1.1).
Overlooking whether the reaction is exothermic (25M.1A.SL.TZ2.16).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct numbers with the wrong sign is a listed distractor, chosen by a quarter in 25M.1A.SL.TZ2.16.

disguises: Organic acid with a three-to-one equation
Temperature written in kelvin
Excess reactant in the stem
3_novel_application.heuristic: Sign from temperature, size from limiting moles, factor from the equation.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ all or nothing; written work allows ECF, and significant figures have cost marks (11M.2.SL.TZ2.1).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Do not convert temperatures: the difference is the same in K and °C.

6_data_booklet.hack: Here the stem gives both c and Q = mcΔT. The sign rule is NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Temperature fall: reject negative ΔH. Temperature rise: reject positive ΔH.
An option smaller by the coefficient has skipped the scaling to the equation.

cards.title: Compare lattice enthalpies: charge first, then ionic radius

walkthrough.question:
Four ionic solids are listed below. Separating one mole of each into gaseous ions takes a different amount of energy. Which solid needs the most energy, meaning it has the highest lattice enthalpy?
A. MgS
B. MgO
C. CaBr2
D. NaF
walkthrough.key_idea: Highest ion charges win first; then smallest ions give the strongest attraction.
walkthrough.question_type: Compare lattice enthalpies from charge and radius
walkthrough.careful: Compare ions' charge and radius, never atomic radius or electronegativity.
procedure: Write each compound's ions with their charges.
Compare ion charges; larger charges attract more strongly.
Keep only the compounds with the largest charges.
Among those, compare ionic radii using group position.
Choose the smaller ions: centres closer, attraction stronger.
tricks: Spot the 2+/2− compound first; it beats 1+/1− and 2+/1−.
Same charges: smaller ions win. Fails if one shrinks, other grows; check section 16.
Section 16 check: MgO is 3791 kJ mol−1, NaF only 930.
if_lost: What does lattice enthalpy measure: which particles are being pulled apart?
What charge does each ion carry, judging by its group?
Which compounds have the largest charges on both ions?
If charges tie, which anion sits higher in its group?

4_command_terms.short: No command term: pick the one largest value.
4_command_terms.why: An MCQ rewards only the final letter, so no reasoning is written. Get the order of checks right, then stop.
4_command_terms.avoid: Trying to recall all four values; two are not even in section 16.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the compound whose ions attract most strongly, judged from charge and size.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, for the correct letter. No working is marked.

1_context.short: Lattice enthalpy is a Born-Haber term; compare it by ion properties.
1_context.why: Lattice enthalpy measures separating a solid into gaseous ions, so its size tracks the attraction between those ions. Only ion charge and distance between ions matter here.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from atomic radii or valence electrons, which examiners reported in trend explanations (12M.2.HL.TZ2.3).
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.5: Born-Haber cycles include lattice enthalpy. Comparing its values is not spelled out there; past papers test it.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show one rule with tidy pairs. This question mixes charge types and sizes, so you must sort by charge before looking at radius.

3_novel_application.short: CaBr2 has three ions, yet 2+/2− pairs still attract more.
3_novel_application.why: Attraction grows with the product of charges and falls with distance. A 2+/2− pair scores four, 2+/1− scores two, 1+/1− scores one. Radius separates similar scores.
3_novel_application.avoid: Choosing by how many ions the formula contains or how heavy the compound looks.
3_novel_application.disguise: Four formulas hide three charge patterns, and the two closest options differ only in their anion.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Rewrite every formula as ions with charges, then rank by charges before looking at any radius.

7_elimination.short: Drop compounds with 1− anions; then S2− loses to smaller O2−.
7_elimination.why: Lower charges mean weaker attraction, so C and D fall. With the same cation and same charges, the larger anion keeps the ions further apart, so A falls.
7_elimination.avoid: Eliminating on electronegativity, a wrong reason examiners flagged in a similar comparison (14M.2.HL.TZ2.8).

definitely_wrong.rule: Both ions are only singly charged, so it cannot beat a 2+/2− pair.
Bromide is only 1− and both ions are large.
Same charges as the other Mg compound, but S2− is larger than O2−.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 16 lists MgO and NaF; it omits MgS and CaBr2.
6_data_booklet.why: The table supports the rule but cannot answer alone. Its series such as MgO to BaO show values falling as ions grow, so you can extend the trend.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for MgS or CaBr2 values in the table: they are not there.
6_data_booklet.pattern: MgO 3791, CaO 3401, SrO 3223, BaO 3054: values fall down a group. NaF is 930, and MgCl2 is 2540 kJ mol−1.
6_data_booklet.memorise: The rule linking charge and radius to lattice enthalpy, and values for MgS and CaBr2, are NOT in section 16. Get charges from group number.

5_time_efficiency.short: Sort by charge, compare one anion pair, done in thirty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Charge sorting removes two options at once, leaving one radius comparison. No values or calculation are needed.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Building a Born-Haber cycle or adding terms; nothing here needs a sum.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip exact values, cycle terms and electronegativity. First ionization energy is not a feature that raises lattice enthalpy (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).

2_markscheme_logic.short: The mark goes to MgO: highest charges and the smaller anion.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Attraction grows with charge and falls with distance between ion centres. Written markschemes credit this distance language for comparisons with the same charges (25M.2.HL.6209.4, 19M.2.HL.TZ1.3).
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Stopping at charge and picking MgS: it ties with MgO on charge, so radius must decide.
trigger_phrases: Letter B alone earns this MCQ mark
Written form: greater distance between ion centres (19M.2.HL.TZ1.3)
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Here the mark stops at the letter. In written answers, the reference must clearly be to ions, not atoms (25M.2.HL.6209.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A and B tie on charge. B wins only because O2− is smaller than S2−, so charge alone stalls at a tie.

walkthrough.answer: B. MgO has 2+ and 2− ions, like MgS, but O2− is smaller than S2−, so its ions are closer and attract most strongly.

1_context.ao: AO2 when ranking compounds in an MCQ; AO3 when explaining a difference in writing.
1_context.syllabus_hook: R1.2.5 names lattice enthalpy as a Born-Haber term. Comparing values is not stated in this understanding; the pattern comes from past papers.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach charge and radius as one short rule. Exams mix charge types, ask for full orderings, and demand the word ionic in written reasons.

trigger_phrases: higher charge and smaller radius of the positive ion (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20)
trap_boundaries: A written radius mark needs a clear reference to ions (25M.2.HL.6209.4).
Lower first ionization energy is not a feature that raises lattice enthalpy (08N.1.HL.TZ0.20).
